name: coga/checkouts
description: The complete checkout lifecycle — which checkout each step starts in (its frozen `checkout:`), launch's branch preparation and handoff, and which checkout to invoke Coga from; reconciliation, the launch boundary, direct chat, the manual procedure, and the sandbox clone live in its leaves.
---

# Feature checkouts

Code-ticket work runs in the checkout the session was launched from. Every
session starts from a clean, current `main`, a step that changes code works
on its feature branch, and the session ends back on `main`. Under
`coga launch` the launcher performs the branch setup and both moves; in any
other session the agent does. Ticket work creates no linked worktrees; the
one alternative checkout is the [sandbox clone fallback](sandbox-clone/SKILL.md).
Only the recurring runner's temporary control worktree and Retro's isolated
checkout (created and removed for one Retro pass) are linked worktrees; ones
left from an earlier layout are disposed of by
[coga/checkout-cleanup](../checkout-cleanup/SKILL.md).

The ticket's `## Dev` record (`branch:`, `worktree:` for a sandbox clone,
`pr:`) is the link from ticket to branch to PR. It is explicit, not inferred
from the slug, because slug conventions break whenever a PR bundles tickets,
an agent picks another branch name, or a slug is truncated. Anything that
follows the link (bump gates, `open-pr`, autoclose, retire, status views)
reads the record; a branch name need not match the slug.

`origin` and `main` stand for the configured `[git].remote` and
`[git].control_branch`; `coga/tasks/`, `coga/recurring/`, and `coga/log.md`
for the configured workspace's task, recurring, and log paths. **The Coga
roots** are the Coga root plus the configured contexts root; every eligible (unignored) file there is Coga state
that publication carries ([coga/state-publication](../state-publication/SKILL.md)).

## Leaves

- [reconciliation](reconciliation/SKILL.md) — keeping edits current with main.
- [launch-boundary](launch-boundary/SKILL.md) — preparing and returning the
  invoking checkout, refusal recovery, and exemptions.
- [chat](chat/SKILL.md) — direct chat's occupancy guard and branch.
- [manual](manual/SKILL.md) — the start, work, and end an agent performs
  when launch did not prepare the branch.
- [sandbox-clone](sandbox-clone/SKILL.md) — the sandbox clone fallback.

## Start, work, end

Main can advance during any session. Follow
[reconciliation](reconciliation/SKILL.md) for the shared freshness and conflict
policy, including documentation, ticket edits, and ad-hoc work.

### Which checkout a step starts in

The frozen step declares its entry. A workflow step may set `checkout:` to one
of four values ([definition format](../workflows/SKILL.md#definition-format)):

- `control` — run from a clean control checkout; no branch.
- `create-or-reuse` — create the task branch, or reuse the recorded one.
- `reuse-required` — reuse the recorded `branch:`; refuse without one.
- `manual` — launch prepares and returns control but sets up no branch and
  says so; the agent follows this topic itself. An omitted field means
  `manual`.

Freezing writes the explicit value on every step, so a declared policy is
authoritative: workflow name, step name, skills, a local edit of the step's
skill or section, `assignee:` and `requires:` do not change it. Customize the
procedure and its instructions freely; the checkout follows the declaration.
The field is data for the shared mechanics below and never bypasses
occupancy, Git, owner-gate or assist checks. Roles and completion gates stay
independent: a `manual` step that `requires: branch` still needs its
`branch:` before bump.

Every frozen `checkout:` value is validated before launch reserves, creates or
switches a branch; only the [launch boundary](launch-boundary/SKILL.md)'s
initial normalization to control precedes that refusal. An invalid value,
on any step, stops the launch and is a `coga validate` error. If the
ticket's workflow or step changes on control while launch prepares, launch
refuses before spawning; retry it.

The packaged workflows declare:

| Workflow | Step | `checkout:` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `code/design-then-implement` | `design`, `evaluate-design`, `review-design` | `control` |
| all five packaged code/docs workflows | `implement` | `create-or-reuse` |
| `code/agent-merge`, `code/design-then-implement`, `code/with-review`, `docs/with-review` | `peer-review` | `reuse-required` |
| `code/with-self-review` | `self-qa` | `reuse-required` |
| `code/agent-merge`, `code/design-then-implement`, `code/with-review`, `docs/with-review` | `open-pr` | `control` |
| `code/with-self-review` | `pr` | `control` |
| `code/agent-merge` | `merge` | `reuse-required` |
| all but `code/agent-merge` | owner-held `review` (an explicit assist) | `reuse-required` |

Every other packaged workflow omits the field and freezes `manual`.

A repo-local copy of a workflow wins over the package. A local copy written
before `checkout:` existed therefore freezes `manual` for new tickets, even
when its name and skills match a packaged code workflow. Declare the policies
in the local definition to restore branch preparation; existing tickets keep
their snapshots.

#### Legacy snapshots

A frozen step **without** a `checkout` key was frozen before the field
existed. For those only, launch keeps the earlier closed table: the packaged
entry above applies when the qualified workflow and step match, and the
instructions the step consumes (its resolved step skill, or its live inline
`## <step>` section) equal the packaged copy. A CRLF checkout of the skill,
as Git for Windows' `core.autocrlf` produces, still matches. Older
`code/with-review` snapshots consume an inline `peer-review` section that
delegates to `code/peer-review`; both must match. Anything else gets
`manual`. The runtime notice and launch report say `legacy snapshot` when
this path selected the entry.

No command rewrites a frozen ticket to add `checkout:`. The fallback may be
deleted only in a reviewed change after no live ticket in supported repos
carries a code/docs snapshot without `checkout:`, or after an explicitly
reviewed migration of those snapshots. Do not rewrite snapshots merely to
delete it.

### In a launched session

An ordinary `coga launch` of an agent-held step (or an explicit assist on an
owner-held step) does this for every step it chains, after bringing the
checkout to current control (the [launch boundary](launch-boundary/SKILL.md)).
It sets `COGA_LAUNCH_RETURNS_CHECKOUT=1` only when it will return the
checkout. The prompt's **Checkout (runtime)** notice states what it observed
and did.

1. **Entry.** For a create step with no `branch:`, launch creates one
   (`coga/<task>-<hex>`) at control and prepares `branch:` under `## Dev`.
   An ordinary agent-only startup publishes that linkage with its final
   lifecycle and launch audit before switching
   ([publication boundaries](../state-publication/launch-boundaries/SKILL.md)).
   Other managed paths retain independent linkage publication. Otherwise it reuses the first
   recorded `branch:`: a local ref as is (a behind one fast-forwards to its
   remote; ahead or diverged commits are kept and reported), or one created
   from its remote tip. It refuses — on control, starting nothing — a
   recorded branch absent everywhere, a reuse step with no branch (unless
   `## Already satisfied` evidence exists: the agent then verifies from
   control), a branch committing ticket intent control lacks ([stranded
   ticket writes](#stranded-ticket-writes)), one held by another worktree,
   or ignored files the switch would overwrite. After switching it projects
   only this ticket from control, unstaged: the session's only entry dirt.
2. **Work.** Commit only code: stage paths by name, never `git add -A` or
   `commit -a`. Never stage, commit, or restore the projected ticket. A
   context, skill, or workflow edit that belongs to the code PR is committed
   with it. Left dirty, it is
   [held for merge](../state-publication/SKILL.md#held-for-merge-on-feature-checkouts):
   the sweep does not publish it, and return refuses until it is committed
   on the branch or redone on control.
   To rebase, first copy the ticket outside the repo and verify the copy,
   restore it from HEAD (delete it if HEAD lacks it), rebase, then write the
   copy back unstaged and compare bytes. Test, commit, rebase onto
   `origin/main`, push.
3. **Hand off from the branch.** Write the handoff in the projected ticket,
   then run `coga bump` last; it publishes the ticket and log. Launch
   returns the checkout to a clean `main` afterwards. A bump that prints
   `[git] sync failed` or `sync refused` left the handoff unpublished, and
   launch's return will refuse over it; say so rather than discarding it.
   The bump itself was recorded, so never bump again to publish it: after a
   `sync failed`, once Git access is restored, run the `coga run
   publish-state` recovery the report prints
   ([recovery](../state-publication/SKILL.md#recovering-a-failed-publication)).
   After a `sync refused` (control's ticket changed meanwhile), preserve the
   handoff and reconcile it onto control's copy
   ([reconciliation](reconciliation/SKILL.md)). An unused prepared branch
   needs no commit or PR when the work proves already satisfied.

A control step sees `main`; publication (`coga open-pr`) reads and pushes the
branch by name from there. A step that must exceptionally change code from
control — a docs publication fix — follows the [manual procedure](manual/SKILL.md).
A preparation failure exits 75 naming the stage and where the checkout
stands; it never rolls back, and the next launch retries the same branch
name. A recorded `worktree:` (a sandbox clone) keeps this primary on control
and names the clone, which must exist on the recorded branch; see
[sandbox-clone](sandbox-clone/SKILL.md).

### Manual or API sessions, megalaunch picks, and exempt checkouts

Without the witness, and before editing in a manual-policy step, the agent
performs the start check, branch work, and end-of-step return itself, and
publishes its pre-branch ticket edits explicitly:
[coga/checkouts/manual](manual/SKILL.md).

The recorded human assist runs on its recorded PR branch under
[coga/human-assist](../human-assist/SKILL.md).

### Direct chat

`coga chat` keeps discussion and routine state edits on control, unstaged.
Before implementation or deliberately reviewed knowledge work it publishes
pending routine state, requires a clean checkout, then runs the notice's
`prepare-checkout` command; [coga/checkouts/chat](chat/SKILL.md) owns that contract.
Knowledge left dirty on the chat's branch is held for merge, and the chat's
return refuses over it.

Launch never changes directory: the session runs where `coga launch` was
invoked, and launch never follows a recorded `worktree:`.

## Which checkout you invoke Coga from

- **Mutating commands publish from wherever they run.** The exit sweep
  publishes dirty and eligible committed state under the Coga roots to
  control, even after a config failure. On a control checkout that is every
  dirty file there. On a feature or detached checkout it is routine state
  only (tickets, the log, recurring runtime state); other files, dirty or
  committed, [wait for merge](../state-publication/SKILL.md#held-for-merge-on-feature-checkouts).
  Write knowledge edits that should land directly on `main`; commit one that
  belongs to a code PR on its branch. Which invocations sweep is
  owned by [coga/state-publication](../state-publication/SKILL.md#when-coga-publishes).
- **`coga launch <target> --prompt-report` regenerates `.agent-skills/`.**
  It skips the state sweep. For a write-free view call
  `compose.compose_prompt_report` or `compose.compose_prompt` directly.
- **Launch and megalaunch compose from the invoking checkout.** An ordinary
  ticket launch or direct chat brings it to fresh control first (the [launch
  boundary](launch-boundary/SKILL.md)). Megalaunch fast-forwards a control
  checkout before queueing ([refresh first](../megalaunch/SKILL.md#refresh-first))
  but only fetches on a feature branch, so run it and exempt launches from a
  control checkout synced to `origin/<control>`; a stale one re-dispatches
  merged work.

## Stranded ticket writes

A ticket write committed on the feature branch strands there: control keeps
rewriting the same file at every transition. `open-pr`'s freshness gate
refuses it and `bump` warns about it on stderr. In a sandbox clone an
uncommitted ticket edit surfaces as `coga open-pr`'s "Recorded worktree has
uncommitted changes" refusal, which names this ticket's file separately.
The comparison is one-directional; a branch copy control already absorbed is
silent. Uncommitted blackboard prose left in another checkout is not
detected; publish it before switching away.

Repair: inspect the branch copy, preserve anything still needed in the primary
ticket, then restore the merge base's copy on the branch and commit:

```sh
git restore --staged --worktree --source=$(git merge-base <control> <branch>) -- <path>
```

Do not rebase to fix it, and do not restore control's copy (it goes stale at
the next transition). A dirty task/log hunk in a sandbox clone is a duplicate
only after its content is preserved in the primary ticket or verified in the
authoritative log; discard only confirmed duplicates, never commit or stash
them to pass the clean-tree gate, and never hand-edit `coga/log.md`.
This ticket's own file is never implementation diff: control has already
rewritten it, so a branch commit of it is an overlapping stranded write. Move
an intentional authored-body change to the live ticket in the primary
checkout and discard the clone's copy. `ticket.py` and other attachments
under `coga/tasks/` do not stay in the diff either: the task directory is
routine state, so a sweeping command run on the feature checkout adopts their
committed branch copies to control (the committed-state boundary in
[coga/state-publication](../state-publication/SKILL.md#control-versus-feature-checkouts)).
Make those changes in the primary checkout's live task, like an authored body
change.

Size exception: the launched lifecycle, the per-step checkout map, and the
invocation and stranded-write rules stay together because each step's
start-and-return contract needs all of them, while the procedures already
live in leaves.

description: Main as the shared source of truth for all agent edits, freshness checkpoints, preserving unique work during reconciliation, and when conflicts need human judgment.
---

# Reconcile work with moving main

The configured remote control branch (`origin/main` by default) is the source of
truth for shared repository state. A local checkout and the launch prompt are
snapshots; expect main to advance during a session. This applies to all agent
edits, including code, documentation, contexts, skills, workflows, tickets,
and bootstrap or ad-hoc work. A fresh launch does not guarantee a fresh handoff.

## Freshness checkpoints

Before editing, fetch current main and inspect changes relevant to the work,
including its governing instructions. Before publishing or handing off edits,
fetch again and reconcile against that tip. Read-only work needs no merge;
qualify conclusions tied to an older revision if relevant files changed.
Git-disabled or remote-less work cannot claim remote freshness; report that
limitation when handing off changes.

## Preserve both sides

Reconciliation preserves main's newer work and the still-needed local intent:

- For committed branch work, merge or rebase current main using the owning
  workflow's procedure ([code branch procedure](../SKILL.md#start-work-end)).
  Resolve straightforward conflicts yourself; a clean Git merge still needs
  inspection for changes in meaning or assumptions.
- For uncommitted edits, inspect the branch's committed changes as well as
  its staged and unstaged deltas and main's intervening changes. Preserve the
  dirty deltas in patches or file copies, including untracked files, and
  record the original branch HEAD. Verify those backups before clearing any
  dirty files. Restore tracked files and the index from the branch's own
  HEAD, merge or rebase current main, then reapply the still-needed dirty
  deltas onto the resulting branch, resolving conflicts there. Do not replace
  a feature file with main's version first: that also removes committed
  branch work which a working-tree patch does not contain.
- For a stale ticket publication or a handoff, preserve unpublished prose
  and blackboard notes before refreshing the ticket from control. Account
  for committed local intent as well as dirty edits; reconcile the intended
  changes onto control's current ticket while respecting CLI-owned lifecycle
  fields. This ticket-specific recovery is not a recipe for replacing code
  files with main's version. Never replay a transition merely because its
  publication failed; use the publication recovery described in the
  [handoff procedure](../SKILL.md#in-a-launched-session).

If any work already landed, prove that from history and content before dropping
the duplicate. Preserve the owning definition and reconcile dependent references.

## Sync a feature branch with control

Every Coga command run from a feature or detached checkout publishes the
ticket and log it changed to control and leaves those files dirty in that
checkout by design ([state publication](../../state-publication/SKILL.md#control-versus-feature-checkouts)).
A new ticket stays untracked. That dirt blocks `git merge` or `git rebase` of
control until it is dropped.

Drop it only when every dirty or untracked file under the Coga and contexts
roots already equals control. Each such file must be a regular file whose
bytes (after clean filters) and mode equal the copy in the local
`<remote>/<control>` ref. A tracked file must also have no staged change.
`coga status` checks this against local refs (fetch first for a current
answer). When it holds, `coga status` prints the exact command, anchored to
the Git root, with paths quoted for the current shell. On POSIX it has this
shape, and any part with no paths is left out:

```bash
git --literal-pathspecs -C <root> checkout -- <tracked…> && rm -- <untracked…> && git -C <root> merge --no-edit <remote>/<control>
```

Native Windows PowerShell gets the same steps with `Remove-Item -LiteralPath`,
each nested in `if ($?) { … }`. `git merge --autostash` is not enough: it sets
aside tracked dirt, but an untracked ticket identical to control still aborts
the merge ("untracked working tree files would be overwritten"). Prefer merge
over rebase for a branch that is already pushed, so it needs no force-push.

When `coga status` instead lists files that differ, are staged, have another
mode, or are deleted, do not use the command. Publish differing routine state
(tickets, the log) first (`coga run publish-state`), then check again. A file
[held for merge](../../state-publication/SKILL.md#held-for-merge-on-feature-checkouts)
cannot be published from the branch: commit it on the branch for review, or
redo it on control. Otherwise reconcile those files by hand as in
[Preserve both sides](#preserve-both-sides).

## Verify and escalate

Inspect the combined diff and run checks appropriate to the affected work
after reconciliation. If publication reports that main moved again, repeat
the comparison against the new tip. Normal movement is not itself a blocker.
Escalate per session conduct when intent conflicts, ownership is unclear, or
access prevents reconciliation; identify the conflicting changes and the
decision or capability needed. Never choose main's entire file blindly,
discard unique work to silence sync, or bypass a publication or lifecycle
guard. These rules do not authorize taking over another task's dirty checkout
or crossing a human approval gate.

activation of a draft reference, freezes its steps. CLI transitions manage step;
do not rewrite a live snapshot or advance it by editing YAML. Frozen example:

      steps:

          skills:                          # Optional procedures for this step; plural, never skill.

Keep current decisions and their reasons, verification, next actions, and
blockers here. Update current values in place instead of appending stale copies.

Optional ## Dev: branch: <name> when created; pr: <full /pull/ URL> when opened;

# Coga's design principles

Coga is an instrument for people directing agents, not another coding
agent. Agents work in sessions; people's goals, questions, and decisions
outlive those sessions. Coga keeps the working plan in text people can
inspect, challenge, and change — including when the right decision is not
to build.

## Principles

- **Expand human capacity.** Expand people's ability to think, explore, and
  create. People choose purpose and direction; agents help discover problems,
  challenge assumptions, and build. Automate mechanical work to leave more
  attention for judgment. People and agents together do not outperform the
  stronger of the two by default; process makes the difference. Route each
  step to whoever is stronger at it, and keep the whole problem in a form
  people can see and restructure, so together they reach what neither reaches
  alone.
- **Text above code.** Readable text carries intent, knowledge, and decisions.
  Code implements that understanding and can be rewritten as we learn.
- **Context is explicit.** People can find, question, correct, and choose the
  knowledge each task needs. Make what an agent works from understandable.
- **Small improvements compound.** Correct the instructions behind an error
  so later work starts from better understanding. Keep changes visible and
  correctable; retain what proves useful and revise what stops working.
- **Yours and hackable.** People own their knowledge and tools. They can
  inspect, change, and move them, reshape how they work, and replace agents.
  The mechanisms serving those freedoms can change too.
- **Keep everything at human scale.** Keep Coga a thin overlay on agent
  capabilities, small enough to inspect and change. The tool should fit the
  way people work, not make them fit its process.
- **Amplify agents, don't duplicate them.** Use existing coding agents to
  plan, research, implement, and review. Coga organizes and carries their
  work across tasks and sessions instead of rebuilding their capabilities.
- **Coga encoded in Coga.** Use the same tickets, contexts, and workflows to
  describe and evolve Coga itself.
- **Fail loud.** Surface missing knowledge and failed operations so people
  can correct them. Never present an unnoticed failure as success.
- **The task outlives the session.** Give substantive work a durable record
  that people can direct and agents can resume.

## Consequences

- **Homoiconicity for agents.** Tickets, contexts, and workflows use the
  same Markdown that agents read and can edit. There is no separate
  agent-only version of the plan.
- **Everything is disposable except the text.** Code and methods can be
  replaced. Intent, decisions, and what we learn survive in editable files.
- **Agents can manage Coga itself.** They can write tickets, revise contexts,
  and change workflows without learning a special language.
- **Build Coga on base concepts agents are good with.** Use familiar tickets,
  plans, and workflows rather than inventing a language agents must learn.

## In practice

Planning serves both people and agents. The agent's proposal gives the human
something concrete to read: the intended outcome, assumptions, approach,
and criteria for success. A human can question its assumptions, correct the
tickets or context, add a review step, or stop the project. The revised text
also directs later agent work. Coga uses the agent's planning capability and
keeps that shared understanding editable across sessions. The
[Coga history examples](../../../../README.md#when-coga-changed-its-own-mind)
show a discarded architectural assumption and a maintenance workflow changed
when it became clear that transient notes would not preserve key findings.

Fresh sessions make written handoffs important. The agent records useful
findings, decisions, and open questions in the
[blackboard](../../../../src/coga/resources/templates/coga/bootstrap/contexts/coga/blackboard/SKILL.md); the next
[launch](../../../../src/coga/resources/templates/coga/bootstrap/contexts/coga/prompt-composition/SKILL.md) starts from the current
files. People can inspect, correct, and share the working knowledge carried
forward. The record can be incomplete or wrong, so its reviewability matters
as much as its persistence. This gives people a practical way to manage
context rot and understand the work they delegate.

Choose knowledge and procedures for their relevance to the task. Explicit
attachment puts selected guidance into the starting prompt; deciding what is
needed, missing, or obsolete remains work for people and agents. The
[research on context and skills](reading-list.md#context-skills-and-plan-review)
supports examining that choice carefully: useful guidance can help, while
irrelevant or conflicting instructions can add cost or hurt results. Those
studies do not establish a performance gain for Coga itself.

These principles guide Coga's design. The
[README](https://github.com/FastJVM/coga/blob/main/README.md) derives from them;
edits to the README must stay aligned. Behavioral topics own current
implementation contracts, including Git. The
[reading list](https://github.com/FastJVM/coga/blob/main/docs/contexts/coga-dev/principles/reading-list.md)
records our influences.

# Feature checkouts

Code-ticket work runs in the checkout the session was launched from. Every
session starts from a clean, current `main`, a step that changes code works
on its feature branch, and the session ends back on `main`. Under
`coga launch` the launcher performs the branch setup and both moves; in any

one alternative checkout is the [sandbox clone fallback](sandbox-clone/SKILL.md).
Only the recurring runner's temporary control worktree and Retro's isolated
checkout (created and removed for one Retro pass) are linked worktrees; ones
left from an earlier layout are disposed of by
[coga/checkout-cleanup](../checkout-cleanup/SKILL.md).

The ticket's `## Dev` record (`branch:`, `worktree:` for a sandbox clone,
`pr:`) is the link from ticket to branch to PR. It is explicit, not inferred
from the slug, because slug conventions break whenever a PR bundles tickets,
an agent picks another branch name, or a slug is truncated. Anything that
follows the link (bump gates, `open-pr`, autoclose, retire, status views)
reads the record; a branch name need not match the slug.

`origin` and `main` stand for the configured `[git].remote` and
`[git].control_branch`; `coga/tasks/`, `coga/recurring/`, and `coga/log.md`
for the configured workspace's task, recurring, and log paths. **The Coga
roots** are the Coga root plus the configured contexts root; every eligible (unignored) file there is Coga state
that publication carries ([coga/state-publication](../state-publication/SKILL.md)).

## Leaves

- [reconciliation](reconciliation/SKILL.md) — keeping edits current with main.
- [launch-boundary](launch-boundary/SKILL.md) — preparing and returning the
  invoking checkout, refusal recovery, and exemptions.
- [chat](chat/SKILL.md) — direct chat's occupancy guard and branch.
- [manual](manual/SKILL.md) — the start, work, and end an agent performs
  when launch did not prepare the branch.
- [sandbox-clone](sandbox-clone/SKILL.md) — the sandbox clone fallback.

[reconciliation](reconciliation/SKILL.md) for the shared freshness and conflict
policy, including documentation, ticket edits, and ad-hoc work.

- `reuse-required` — reuse the recorded `branch:`; refuse without one.
- `manual` — launch prepares and returns control but sets up no branch and
  says so; the agent follows this topic itself. An omitted field means
  `manual`.

Freezing writes the explicit value on every step, so a declared policy is
authoritative: workflow name, step name, skills, a local edit of the step's
skill or section, `assignee:` and `requires:` do not change it. Customize the
procedure and its instructions freely; the checkout follows the declaration.
The field is data for the shared mechanics below and never bypasses
occupancy, Git, owner-gate or assist checks. Roles and completion gates stay
independent: a `manual` step that `requires: branch` still needs its
`branch:` before bump.

## Stranded ticket writes

A ticket write committed on the feature branch strands there: control keeps
rewriting the same file at every transition. `open-pr`'s freshness gate
refuses it and `bump` warns about it on stderr. In a sandbox clone an
uncommitted ticket edit surfaces as `coga open-pr`'s "Recorded worktree has
uncommitted changes" refusal, which names this ticket's file separately.
The comparison is one-directional; a branch copy control already absorbed is
silent. Uncommitted blackboard prose left in another checkout is not
detected; publish it before switching away.

Repair: inspect the branch copy, preserve anything still needed in the primary
ticket, then restore the merge base's copy on the branch and commit:

```sh
git restore --staged --worktree --source=$(git merge-base <control> <branch>) -- <path>
```

Do not rebase to fix it, and do not restore control's copy (it goes stale at
the next transition). A dirty task/log hunk in a sandbox clone is a duplicate
only after its content is preserved in the primary ticket or verified in the
authoritative log; discard only confirmed duplicates, never commit or stash
them to pass the clean-tree gate, and never hand-edit `coga/log.md`.
This ticket's own file is never implementation diff: control has already
rewritten it, so a branch commit of it is an overlapping stranded write. Move
an intentional authored-body change to the live ticket in the primary
checkout and discard the clone's copy. `ticket.py` and other attachments
under `coga/tasks/` do not stay in the diff either: the task directory is
routine state, so a sweeping command run on the feature checkout adopts their
committed branch copies to control (the committed-state boundary in
[coga/state-publication](../state-publication/SKILL.md#control-versus-feature-checkouts)).
Make those changes in the primary checkout's live task, like an authored body
change.

Size exception: the launched lifecycle, the per-step checkout map, and the
invocation and stranded-write rules stay together because each step's
start-and-return contract needs all of them, while the procedures already
live in leaves.

# Reconcile work with moving main

The configured remote control branch (`origin/main` by default) is the source of
truth for shared repository state. A local checkout and the launch prompt are
snapshots; expect main to advance during a session. This applies to all agent
edits, including code, documentation, contexts, skills, workflows, tickets,
and bootstrap or ad-hoc work. A fresh launch does not guarantee a fresh handoff.

## Freshness checkpoints

Before editing, fetch current main and inspect changes relevant to the work,
including its governing instructions. Before publishing or handing off edits,
fetch again and reconcile against that tip. Read-only work needs no merge;
qualify conclusions tied to an older revision if relevant files changed.
Git-disabled or remote-less work cannot claim remote freshness; report that
limitation when handing off changes.

## Preserve both sides

Reconciliation preserves main's newer work and the still-needed local intent:

- For committed branch work, merge or rebase current main using the owning
  workflow's procedure ([code branch procedure](../SKILL.md#start-work-end)).
  Resolve straightforward conflicts yourself; a clean Git merge still needs
  inspection for changes in meaning or assumptions.
- For uncommitted edits, inspect the branch's committed changes as well as
  its staged and unstaged deltas and main's intervening changes. Preserve the
  dirty deltas in patches or file copies, including untracked files, and
  record the original branch HEAD. Verify those backups before clearing any
  dirty files. Restore tracked files and the index from the branch's own
  HEAD, merge or rebase current main, then reapply the still-needed dirty
  deltas onto the resulting branch, resolving conflicts there. Do not replace
  a feature file with main's version first: that also removes committed
  branch work which a working-tree patch does not contain.
- For a stale ticket publication or a handoff, preserve unpublished prose
  and blackboard notes before refreshing the ticket from control. Account
  for committed local intent as well as dirty edits; reconcile the intended
  changes onto control's current ticket while respecting CLI-owned lifecycle
  fields. This ticket-specific recovery is not a recipe for replacing code
  files with main's version. Never replay a transition merely because its
  publication failed; use the publication recovery described in the
  [handoff procedure](../SKILL.md#in-a-launched-session).

If any work already landed, prove that from history and content before dropping
the duplicate. Preserve the owning definition and reconcile dependent references.

## Sync a feature branch with control

Every Coga command run from a feature or detached checkout publishes the
ticket and log it changed to control and leaves those files dirty in that
checkout by design ([state publication](../../state-publication/SKILL.md#control-versus-feature-checkouts)).
A new ticket stays untracked. That dirt blocks `git merge` or `git rebase` of
control until it is dropped.

Drop it only when every dirty or untracked file under the Coga and contexts
roots already equals control. Each such file must be a regular file whose
bytes (after clean filters) and mode equal the copy in the local
`<remote>/<control>` ref. A tracked file must also have no staged change.
`coga status` checks this against local refs (fetch first for a current
answer). When it holds, `coga status` prints the exact command, anchored to
the Git root, with paths quoted for the current shell. On POSIX it has this
shape, and any part with no paths is left out:

```bash
git --literal-pathspecs -C <root> checkout -- <tracked…> && rm -- <untracked…> && git -C <root> merge --no-edit <remote>/<control>
```

Native Windows PowerShell gets the same steps with `Remove-Item -LiteralPath`,
each nested in `if ($?) { … }`. `git merge --autostash` is not enough: it sets
aside tracked dirt, but an untracked ticket identical to control still aborts
the merge ("untracked working tree files would be overwritten"). Prefer merge
over rebase for a branch that is already pushed, so it needs no force-push.

When `coga status` instead lists files that differ, are staged, have another
mode, or are deleted, do not use the command. Publish differing routine state
(tickets, the log) first (`coga run publish-state`), then check again. A file
[held for merge](../../state-publication/SKILL.md#held-for-merge-on-feature-checkouts)
cannot be published from the branch: commit it on the branch for review, or
redo it on control. Otherwise reconcile those files by hand as in
[Preserve both sides](#preserve-both-sides).

## Verify and escalate

Inspect the combined diff and run checks appropriate to the affected work
after reconciliation. If publication reports that main moved again, repeat
the comparison against the new tip. Normal movement is not itself a blocker.
Escalate per session conduct when intent conflicts, ownership is unclear, or
access prevents reconciliation; identify the conflicting changes and the
decision or capability needed. Never choose main's entire file blindly,
discard unique work to silence sync, or bypass a publication or lifecycle
guard. These rules do not authorize taking over another task's dirty checkout
or crossing a human approval gate.

# Manual start, work, end

Part of [coga/checkouts](../SKILL.md), which owns the launched lifecycle and
which checkout each step starts in.

## Procedure

Use this when no `COGA_LAUNCH_RETURNS_CHECKOUT=1` witness is set — manual or
API sessions, megalaunch picks, exempt checkouts — and before editing in a
step whose runtime notice says launch set up no branch (manual policy, or a
control step that must exceptionally change code). The agent performs both
moves:

1. **Start check.** `git fetch origin main`, then require HEAD on `main`, a
   clean tree with Coga state included, and a successful `git merge
   --ff-only origin/main`. Launch regenerates the ignored
   `coga/.agent-skills/` view; a repo initialized before `coga init` wrote
   that ignore rule sees it as dirt — add `.agent-skills/` to
   `coga/.gitignore`, never commit it. Anything else — dirty files, another
   ticket's branch, a diverged `main` — means stop: ask the attending human,
   or `coga block` in a queue run. Do not work around an occupied checkout
   with a linked worktree, a control checkout, a stash, or a switch.
2. **Work.** Write ticket state (`branch:` under `## Dev` once created with
   `git branch <name>`, plan notes) on `main`, publish it (below), then
   switch to the feature branch and change code only; ticket edits made
   there are not published until the next sweep. A resumed branch is reused:
   switch to it and `git rebase` onto fetched `origin/main`.
3. **End.** Commit, push the branch (`git push -u origin <branch>`, or
   `--force-with-lease` after a rebase), then return:
   - `git fetch origin main`;
   - for every dirty path under the Coga roots, verify it is already on
     `origin/main` by the rules of
     [the launch boundary](../launch-boundary/SKILL.md) (`git diff --quiet origin/main -- <path>`;
     for `coga/log.md`, every added line is on `origin/main`) and discard it
     (`git restore --source=HEAD --staged --worktree -- <path>`). `git diff`
     skips untracked files, so compare an untracked one with
     `git show origin/main:<path> | cmp - <path>` and delete it only when
     identical;
   - `git switch main`, then `git merge --ff-only origin/main`.

   If any dirty path under the Coga roots is *not* already on `origin/main`,
   or any other path is dirty, stop and escalate. A knowledge file the sweep
   [held for merge](../../state-publication/SKILL.md#held-for-merge-on-feature-checkouts)
   belongs in the branch's commit (or redone on `main`), not discarded. Never discard unpublished
   state. Then write the step's handoff on `main` and run `coga bump`, which
   publishes it. The session leaves the checkout on `main`, clean.

## Publish pre-branch ticket edits

Writing `branch:` or plan notes on `main` does not publish them: Git carries
uncommitted edits across a branch switch. Before switching, publish those
edits strictly, naming each edited file. The recipe resolves paths against
the current directory, which launch preserves, so anchor them at the checkout
root:

```sh
coga run publish-state "$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)/coga/tasks/<slug>.md"
git status --porcelain --untracked-files=all
```

Exit 0 means every named file is confirmed on control; any non-zero exit
(contract in [strict publication on
demand](../../state-publication/SKILL.md#strict-publication-on-demand))
is the stop signal. Use the status check only for dirty files you did not name,
and require it to be empty before switching. Do not fall back to calling the
sweep through a `python -c` one-liner: the sweep reports publication failures
without raising, and the shell's `python` often cannot import Coga at all. If
publication fails or the tree remains dirty, stop and escalate; do not switch,
stash, or commit the ticket edit on the feature branch. The same publication applies to a
sandbox clone's `worktree:` record in the primary checkout, before starting
work in the clone.

"""The single implementation of Coga task deletion.

Two spellings, one body: `coga delete <task>` (which adds the resolution
flags and the control-branch sync every other state mutation performs) and the
`delete-task` registered recipe, `coga run delete-task <task>` (the bare
working-tree removal, which is also what the `bootstrap/delete-task` skill
contract names). Recovery is via `git restore`; git history is the audit
trail, so deletion posts no Slack broadcast.

Both task shapes are handled, keyed off the resolved ticket path:

- **Directory form** (`<dir>/ticket.md`) — removes that one task directory and
  nothing else, after confirming it holds the ticket.
- **File form** (`tasks/<slug>.md`) — removes that single file only. It never
  touches the parent (a shared `tasks/` subtree), so a self-contained task can
  be deleted without risking its neighbours.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import shutil
import sys
from pathlib import Path

from coga import git
from coga.config import Config
from coga.tasks import TaskNotFoundError, TaskRef, resolve_task


class DeleteTaskError(RuntimeError):
    """Task deletion refused to remove its target, or could not complete it."""


def run_delete_task(cfg: Config, ref: TaskRef) -> str:
    """Delete one resolved task and return the report line.

    The filesystem removal owns the checkout-local spawn-admission barrier.
    Callers own Git publication: `coga delete` lands the removal immediately;
    recurring replacement recreates the task at the same path and syncs that
    replacement as one state transition.

    `DeleteTaskError` is the *only* failure this raises. Deletion used to run
    behind a subprocess, where a filesystem error surfaced as a non-zero exit
    and became one; in-process, `rmtree`/`unlink` raise `OSError` directly, so
    it is translated here. Every caller — `coga delete`, the recipe, and
    recurring replacement, which runs unattended — catches that one type, and a
    read-only file or a held handle must not abort them with a traceback.
    """
    ticket = ref.ticket_path
    try:
        with git.state_lock(cfg):
            if not ticket.is_file():
                raise DeleteTaskError(
                    f"{ticket} is not a file — refusing to delete"
                )
            if ticket.name == "ticket.md":
                # Directory form: remove the whole task directory (ticket + siblings).
                shutil.rmtree(ticket.parent)
                target: Path = ticket.parent
            else:
                # File form: remove just the single-file ticket; leave the parent
                # (a shared tasks/ subtree) untouched.
                ticket.unlink()
                target = ticket
    except git.GitError as exc:
        raise DeleteTaskError(
            f"could not serialize deletion of {ticket}: {exc}"
        ) from exc
    except OSError as exc:
        raise DeleteTaskError(f"could not delete {ticket}: {exc}") from exc

    return f"{ref.id_slug}: deleted {target}\n"


def run_delete_task_recipe(cfg: Config, argv: list[str]) -> int:
    """`coga run delete-task <task>` — remove one task from the working tree.

    The removal only; landing it on the control branch is `coga delete`'s job.
    """
    if len(argv) != 1 or not argv[0].strip():
        sys.stderr.write(
            "Usage: coga run delete-task <task> — exactly one task ref is "
            f"required (got {len(argv)}).\n"
        )
        return 2

    try:
        ref = resolve_task(cfg, argv[0].strip())
    except TaskNotFoundError as exc:
        sys.stderr.write(f"delete-task: {exc}\n")
        return 2

    try:
        report = run_delete_task(cfg, ref)
    except DeleteTaskError as exc:
        sys.stderr.write(f"delete-task: {exc}\n")
        return 2

    sys.stdout.write(report)
    return 0


__all__ = ["DeleteTaskError", "run_delete_task", "run_delete_task_recipe"]
"""`coga delete` — remove a task directory from the working tree.

Thin entrypoint: resolve the task argument, then call `coga.delete_task`, the
single implementation of task deletion — equally reachable as the registered
`delete-task` recipe. What this command adds on top is the control-branch
sync. Recovery is via `git restore`.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import sys

import typer

from coga import git
from coga.paths import log_path
from coga.config import ConfigError, load_config
from coga.delete_task import DeleteTaskError, run_delete_task
from coga.tasks import TaskNotFoundError, resolve_task


def delete(
    task: str = typer.Argument(..., help="Task ID or id-slug."),
    keep_control_checkout: bool = typer.Option(
        False,
        "--keep-control-checkout",
        help=(
            "From a linked worktree, push the deletion without fast-forwarding "
            "another checkout that holds the control branch. Used by Retro."
        ),
    ),
) -> None:
    """Remove a task directory. Recovery is via `git restore`."""
    try:
        cfg = load_config()
    except ConfigError as exc:
        _bail(str(exc))

    try:
        ref = resolve_task(cfg, task)
    except TaskNotFoundError as exc:
        _bail(str(exc))

    if keep_control_checkout and not git.is_linked_worktree(ref.path):
        _bail(
            "--keep-control-checkout requires a linked git worktree; refusing "
            "to delete from the primary checkout"
        )

    try:
        output = run_delete_task(cfg, ref)
    except DeleteTaskError as exc:
        _bail(str(exc))
    if output:
        typer.echo(output, nl=False)

    # Sync the removal to the control branch, the git analogue of the Slack
    # broadcast every other state mutation posts. Without this, `coga delete`
    # leaves an uncommitted working-tree deletion — the one command that
    # bypassed the sync layer (create/mark/bump/block all call it). The task
    # dir is gone now; `publish` lands the deletion from the working tree's
    # `git status`, and `fast_forward=False` is Retro's isolated delete: leave
    # the operator's control checkout untouched after the remote landing.
    try:
        git.publish(
            cfg,
            [ref.path, log_path(cfg)],
            f"Ticket: {ref.id_slug} — deleted",
            fast_forward=not keep_control_checkout,
        )
    except git.GitError as exc:
        typer.secho(
            git.sync_failure_report(
                cfg, exc, retained="The local deletion was retained"
            ).rstrip("\n"),
            fg=typer.colors.YELLOW,
            err=True,
        )


def _bail(msg: str) -> None:
    typer.secho(msg, fg=typer.colors.RED, err=True)
    sys.exit(2)
Retire the canceled ticket `{slug}`.

Retire is the slug-targeted launcher for `retro/done-ticket` on a canceled
ticket. A done ticket never reaches this task: its positive learning landed
with its merged PR, so `coga retire` deletes it deterministically. A canceled
ticket's learning is negative — the cancellation reason in `coga/log.md` and
anything its body or blackboard records about what did not work, what was
declined and why, and what would reopen it — and nothing has landed it. Retro
extracts that, then deletes the ticket. When new durable knowledge exists,
Retro opens a PR that records the `## Retro` marker, edits the knowledge base,
and deletes the source task directory in the same PR. When no new durable
knowledge exists, Retro uses the deletion route in the skill's **Inbound references** section, with no marker.
This task is the ad-hoc shell that drives that single skill against the named slug. Do not
invent additional steps. The complete Retro pass runs in one subagent inside a
dedicated isolated checkout; do not run it in this retire task's checkout.
`coga retire` tries to dispose of this ticket's own recorded checkout and
branch before launching this task, but skips that cleanup when Git is
disabled or absent, when it runs off the control branch, or after a Git or
read error. Do not assume the recorded checkout or branch is gone.
Other branch hygiene belongs to the `branch-sweep` and `autoclose-merged`
recurring jobs, not this task.

### Console Progress

Write short progress updates to the console before and after each phase: retro
result, PR open when applicable, final status mark. Include the slug or PR link
being acted on. The blackboard remains the durable record; console progress is
for the human watching the run.

### Ordered Pass

Run these in order. Stop and ask if any precondition fails — do not improvise.

1. **Run `retro/done-ticket` against canceled `{slug}`.**

   passing `{slug}`, the snapshot path, and this task's absolute repo root. Use

   or commit it. In the
   isolated subagent, read the skill at
   package `bootstrap/skills/retro/done-ticket/SKILL.md` unless a local
   `coga/skills/retro/done-ticket/SKILL.md` override exists, and follow it.
   The skill verifies the isolated-checkout boundary before reading the snapshot;
   all Retro branch switches and deletes stay inside it. When new durable
   knowledge exists, Retro opens a PR that records the `## Retro` marker, edits
   the knowledge base, and deletes `coga/tasks/{slug}/` in the same PR. When no
   new durable knowledge exists, it runs
   `coga delete {slug} --keep-control-checkout` from a linked worktree or
   ordinary `coga delete {slug}` from an independent clone. Both land the
   direct `Ticket: {slug} — deleted` commit on the remote control branch
   without refreshing the operator's checkout, with no PR and no marker.
   The exception is a ticket that some tracked file still links. It leaves in
   a reference-pin PR that repoints the link to a commit permalink (the skill's
   **Inbound references**). Recovery is via `git restore`.

   After the subagent returns or terminates, read `progress.md`. Without its
   `complete` line, record a partial outcome and retain the run directory and
   isolated checkout. A missing action receipt does not prove the remote was
   unchanged; follow the skill's reconciliation checks before retrying, and
   escalate if the outcome cannot be established. Do not mark this retire task
   done or remove recovery paths on the strength of a final message alone.

   For a completed run, verify the PR branch is pushed or the direct
   deletion is present on the remote control branch, and verify the isolated
   checkout is clean. Remove the copied `coga.local.toml`; then remove the
   linked worktree and its temporary branch, or delete the exact independent
   clone directory. Record the verified outcome on this task's blackboard,
   then delete the temporary run directory (snapshot and progress file) too.
   Mutating subagents are
   not guaranteed to auto-clean. If durability or cleanup cannot be verified,
   preserve both paths and block.

2. **Mark this retire task done.** Run `coga mark done <this-task-slug>`
   with a `--message` summarizing what happened: the retro PR link, or
   "direct-deleted, no durable knowledge or inbound references" for a direct delete.

### Stop conditions

- Source task is not `status: canceled` → escalate via `coga block` with the
  reason. This task only runs Retro on a canceled ticket.
- Source task is missing → first decide **which** kind of missing. If the slug
  is wrong or unknown, escalate.

  Otherwise ask two questions in order.

  **Is it gone from the control branch?** That branch is the authority, not
  your working tree. Retro direct-deletes from a linked worktree with
  `coga delete --keep-control-checkout`, which deliberately leaves the
  operator's checkout untouched, so the source directory can still sit on your
  disk while already being absent from `<remote>/<control-branch>`. Requiring
  absence in both places would send this shell into a Retro run whose fresh
  isolated base lacks the source — which stops, recreating exactly the blocker
  this path exists to avoid. Fetch and check the control branch; a stale local
  copy is not evidence that the task is still live.

  **Did Retro actually process it?** Absence alone does not answer this. Every
  deletion — Retro's and an ordinary user's `coga delete <slug>` — writes the
  same `Ticket: <slug> — deleted` subject, so that commit being an ancestor of
  the control branch proves the directory is gone, not that any knowledge was
  extracted. Closing on the generic commit alone would silently skip Retro and
  discard durable knowledge. Require evidence that ties the deletion to a
  Retro/Dream pass, such as:
  - the deleting commit (or its PR) also adds or updates the source task's
    `## Retro` marker — the knowledge-bearing route;
  - a Dream run's `## Findings` / `## Dream Run Summary`, or a retro PR body,
    naming this slug as processed;
  - a `coga/log.md` line or retro PR recording the no-durable-knowledge
    direct-delete for this slug.

  **orphaned, not broken**: retire's whole contract — knowledge extracted,
  ticket deleted — is already satisfied by the skill this shell exists to
  drive. Record the evidence on this shell's blackboard and `coga mark done`
  it as already satisfied. Do **not** `git restore` the source to rerun Retro,
  and do **not** `coga block` — the missing-source stop condition guards
  against a wrong slug, not against a retirement that already happened.

  With absence but **no** Retro evidence, something deleted the ticket without
  extracting from it. Do not mark this shell done; escalate via `coga block`
  naming the slug and the bare deletion commit, so a human decides whether to
  restore and rerun Retro.
- A complete evidence snapshot, machine-local config copy, or isolated
  worktree/clone execution is unavailable → escalate; never run Retro in this
  task's checkout as a fallback.
- Retro skill stops and asks → surface the reason; do not improvise.
- Anything outside the allowed scope above → escalate, do not improvise.

# Coga microkernel boundary

The [microkernel objectives](objectives/SKILL.md) own the target architecture:
behavior carried by editable tickets, a small generic command surface, and a
program more contributors can understand. The rules below describe the current
boundary; the objectives guide review of its future shape.

## The microkernel rule

Code earns a permanent home in `src/coga/` in two ways. Existing command
heads awaiting that decision are recorded under “Open command placements” below.

1. **Shared infra with at least two real consumers**: compose, config,
   task/ticket IO, the launch machinery, shared parsers and gates (for example
   the `## Dev` parsers and `gh` helpers in `autoclose.py`).
2. **A reviewed, co-versioned command contract**: a function in the fixed
   `runner.RECIPES` registry, or a command whose contract names the
   package-private invariant or atomic transaction that an edge implementation
   using stable CLI and filesystem interfaces could not preserve. Python logic,
   operands, validation, or already living in `src/coga/` rule out alias sugar
   but do not by themselves prove a core home.

Everything else stays at the edge. A single-consumer helper lives beside the
ticket or skill that uses it, or in the wheel-distributed `src/coga_edge/`
package, and imports only appropriate shared core infra. Edge shipping does
not confer kernel status. Production `src/coga/` never imports or path-loads
`coga_edge` or ticket/skill implementations; repo shims choose their imports.
Distribution, upgrades and overrides are owned by
[coga/edge-code](../../../../src/coga/resources/templates/coga/bootstrap/contexts/coga/edge-code/SKILL.md). Skills are invocation contracts and
never executable launch plugins.

- **Count callers of one symbol, not copies of one body.** Three
  byte-identical private `append_report` helpers (`skill_update.py`,
  `dream_validate_drift.py`, `dream_cleanup_orphan_markers.py`) are three
  single-consumer copies. A helper earns a shared home only when the change
  that adds it migrates the existing duplicates onto it in the same PR.
- **The consumer test can keep a symbol in core.** When an implementation
  moves to the edge, any helper it shares with another core consumer stays.

## Open command placements

`megalaunch` is not the only in-package command whose permanent home is
unsettled. The following command heads have no `runner.RECIPES` entry or
ratified command-specific co-versioning proof. Their existing package
residence is provisional; registration as a built-in, Python logic, side
effects, or calling shared infrastructure does not settle their placement.

| Command surface | Open decision | Cleanup ticket |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `megalaunch`, `slack` | Placement of queue orchestration and the user-facing notification head | `work-orchestration-commands-to-tickets` |
| `ticket` | Whether the authoring coordinator requires co-versioning or can live at the edge | `residual-command-surfaces` |
| `show`, `status`, `validate`, `usage`, `recurring list` | Placement of the read/report heads, separately from shared rendering and validation infrastructure | `read-report-commands-as-ticket-workflows` |
| `secret get`, `uninstall` | Placement of acquisition/inspection and removal tooling, separately from launch-time secret injection | `support-commands-boundary` |
| `skill *` | Explicit tooling classification; excluded from the current migration push, without a ratified permanent package-home proof | `residual-command-surfaces` |
| `owner` | Placement of the ticket-owner reassignment head (a `mark`-shaped locked write of `owner:`) | `lifecycle-verbs-to-ticket-operations` |
| `recurring promote` | Placement of the task-to-template move | `residual-command-surfaces` (scope proposed by the refresh) |

These tickets live under `coga/tasks/v1/microkernel/`; the owner's
2026-11-12 decision in [current direction](../current-direction/SKILL.md)
pulled this cleanup back into v1. Emptying this table is a v1 gate.
Commands stay where they are until a reviewed change settles their placement,
and the tickets retain the target
kernel boundary below rather than replacing it. Shared helpers and launch-time
trust hooks retain their own kernel justification independently of the
user-facing heads that call them.

The `owner` head's claim to core is its package-private transaction: it holds
`git.state_lock` across the read, prospective validation, local byte
comparison, write, audit, and strict publication with the original ticket
bytes as `expect`. A concurrent local edit is preserved. A definite
publication failure restores only the command's own ticket bytes and retracts
its audit; an uncertain push keeps the write for reconciliation. Both exit 75
to suppress the generic sweep. With Git disabled or unavailable through a
documented soft-skip, the local write remains the result
([publish primitive](../internals/state-publication/publish/SKILL.md)).

## The `ticket.py` script phase

The user contract is [coga/script-tickets](../../../../src/coga/resources/templates/coga/bootstrap/contexts/coga/script-tickets/SKILL.md).
Owner-accepted design (2026-08-18, PR #700); do not re-argue it without
engaging these reasons:

- **Agent work is deduced from completion, not declared.** Whether the agent
  half runs depends only on whether the script completed its own step, never
  on a static signal such as "the step declares skills". A forgotten
  completion fails toward running the agent (visible, costs tokens, skips
  nothing), never toward silently skipping it. For the same reason launch
  never advances a step on the script's behalf.
- **`ticket.py`, not `run.py`.** A task directory also holds attachments, and
  a `run.py` repro script is a likely accidental trigger; nobody attaches a
  `ticket.py` by accident. The executable bit is ignored because `ls`, GitHub
  and zips do not show or keep it.
- **A stat, not a plugin host.** PR #670's objection ("no plugin host, no
  recursive discovery") does not apply: this is one `stat()` at one fixed path
  inside the target's own directory, affecting only that target, with no scan
  or registry, and core subprocesses the file rather than importing it.
- **Trust caveat, recorded rather than hidden.** A `ticket.py` is a
  git-tracked file reviewed in the PR that adds it, but it runs arbitrary code
  at launch. In a repo where `coga/tasks/**` is granted or reviewed more
  loosely than `src/coga/**`, adding it widens who can cause code to execute
  during launch. Coga's own trust model treats both as "anyone who can write
  this repo", so its threat model does not move; a team that splits those
  permissions should know it.

Source map: `launch_script.script_entry_point` is the classifier;
`run_script_phase` runs one phase (secrets via `build_launch_env`) and
`run_script_chain` chains phases with agent steps. Exit 75 is
`git.RETRY_WITHOUT_SWEEP_EXIT_CODE`. Attribution reads
`task_env.is_script_task`; `task_env.TASK_ENV_KEYS` is the namespace,
cleared by `apply_task_env` and set by `build_task_env`.

## Migrating a built-in to the edge

A stateless verb outside the launch closure and recipe table, with no
co-versioning proof, moves without changing semantics: keep shared parsers,
preflights, and declarative gates (such as `requires: pr` in `bump`) in core
when they have other consumers; keep tests pointed at the moved code with the
same failure behavior; expose the bootstrap target and add an alias only for a
stable spelling; never create a task per invocation.

## The kernel tier and its edges

The kernel is launch/compose and what launch calls mid-flight (`mark`, `bump`,
secret injection, notify dispatch), what must exist before any launch
(`create`, fresh `init`), the `block`/`unblock` state transitions, the fixed
`runner.RECIPES`, thin heads over a fixed recipe (`delete` over `delete-task`,
bare `recurring` over `recurring-scan`), and proven co-versioned commands.
[coga/extension-model](../../../../src/coga/resources/templates/coga/bootstrap/contexts/coga/extension-model/SKILL.md) owns the tiers a
repo chooses from.

- **No inversion.** Moving logic out of the kernel moves the substance
  unchanged: deterministic Python stays Python (a recipe or `ticket.py`),
  never agent judgment.
- **`prepare-checkout` is a recipe, not shared infra alone.** It is the one
  in-chat consumer of the branch preparation in `src/coga/checkouts.py` that
  ordinary launch also calls, so those mechanics are shared infra. The recipe
  is registered because its argv, report and 0/2/75 exits must agree with
  launch's private live-chat receipt. It is not a Typer head, alias, ticket
  plugin, or general phase registry.
- **Skill provenance at use is unbuilt.** Compose does not verify loaded
  skills against a provenance digest; that launch-time trust hook would be
  kernel when built.
- **Keep the bad-alias escape hatch.** `aliases.validate_aliases` failing
  makes `cli.main` exit 2 before ordinary commands. `uninstall` dispatches
  before alias validation runs; `init` and the `recurring --all` parent catch
  the error, warn, and fall back to `aliases.DEFAULT_ALIASES`. Keep both seams
  when tightening validation.

## Edge packaging invariants

`src/coga_edge/` ships in the same wheel as `src/coga/`. Edge modules may
import shared `coga` infrastructure; core never imports edge implementations.
`coga_edge/__init__.py` has no eager job imports or side effects. Phone-home's
module imports only stdlib and shared `coga.*`, never relative or sibling
edge modules, and carries both normal and private `--worker` dispatch behind
`__main__`; its worker executes that same file, including when copied to a
local fork. Preserve these constraints when refactoring it.

# Manual start, work, end

Part of [coga/checkouts](../SKILL.md), which owns the launched lifecycle and
which checkout each step starts in.

## Procedure

Use this when no `COGA_LAUNCH_RETURNS_CHECKOUT=1` witness is set — manual or
API sessions, megalaunch picks, exempt checkouts — and before editing in a
step whose runtime notice says launch set up no branch (manual policy, or a
control step that must exceptionally change code). The agent performs both
moves:

1. **Start check.** `git fetch origin main`, then require HEAD on `main`, a
   clean tree with Coga state included, and a successful `git merge
   --ff-only origin/main`. Launch regenerates the ignored
   `coga/.agent-skills/` view; a repo initialized before `coga init` wrote
   that ignore rule sees it as dirt — add `.agent-skills/` to
   `coga/.gitignore`, never commit it. Anything else — dirty files, another
   ticket's branch, a diverged `main` — means stop: ask the attending human,
   or `coga block` in a queue run. Do not work around an occupied checkout
   with a linked worktree, a control checkout, a stash, or a switch.
2. **Work.** Write ticket state (`branch:` under `## Dev` once created with
   `git branch <name>`, plan notes) on `main`, publish it (below), then
   switch to the feature branch and change code only; ticket edits made
   there are not published until the next sweep. A resumed branch is reused:
   switch to it and `git rebase` onto fetched `origin/main`.
3. **End.** Commit, push the branch (`git push -u origin <branch>`, or
   `--force-with-lease` after a rebase), then return:
   - `git fetch origin main`;
   - for every dirty path under the Coga roots, verify it is already on
     `origin/main` by the rules of
     [the launch boundary](../launch-boundary/SKILL.md) (`git diff --quiet origin/main -- <path>`;
     for `coga/log.md`, every added line is on `origin/main`) and discard it
     (`git restore --source=HEAD --staged --worktree -- <path>`). `git diff`
     skips untracked files, so compare an untracked one with
     `git show origin/main:<path> | cmp - <path>` and delete it only when
     identical;
   - `git switch main`, then `git merge --ff-only origin/main`.

   If any dirty path under the Coga roots is *not* already on `origin/main`,
   or any other path is dirty, stop and escalate. A knowledge file the sweep
   [held for merge](../../state-publication/SKILL.md#held-for-merge-on-feature-checkouts)
   belongs in the branch's commit (or redone on `main`), not discarded. Never discard unpublished
   state. Then write the step's handoff on `main` and run `coga bump`, which
   publishes it. The session leaves the checkout on `main`, clean.

## Publish pre-branch ticket edits

Writing `branch:` or plan notes on `main` does not publish them: Git carries
uncommitted edits across a branch switch. Before switching, publish those
edits strictly, naming each edited file. The recipe resolves paths against
the current directory, which launch preserves, so anchor them at the checkout
root:

```sh
coga run publish-state "$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)/coga/tasks/<slug>.md"
git status --porcelain --untracked-files=all
```

Exit 0 means every named file is confirmed on control; any non-zero exit
(contract in [strict publication on
demand](../../state-publication/SKILL.md#strict-publication-on-demand))
is the stop signal. Use the status check only for dirty files you did not name,
and require it to be empty before switching. Do not fall back to calling the
sweep through a `python -c` one-liner: the sweep reports publication failures
without raising, and the shell's `python` often cannot import Coga at all. If
publication fails or the tree remains dirty, stop and escalate; do not switch,
stash, or commit the ticket edit on the feature branch. The same publication applies to a
sandbox clone's `worktree:` record in the primary checkout, before starting
work in the clone.

Both task shapes are handled, keyed off the resolved ticket path:

- **Directory form** (`<dir>/ticket.md`) — removes that one task directory and

- **File form** (`tasks/<slug>.md`) — removes that single file only. It never
  touches the parent (a shared `tasks/` subtree), so a self-contained task can
  be deleted without risking its neighbours.

from __future__ import annotations

import shutil
import sys
from pathlib import Path

from coga import git
from coga.config import Config
from coga.tasks import TaskNotFoundError, TaskRef, resolve_task


class DeleteTaskError(RuntimeError):
    """Task deletion refused to remove its target, or could not complete it."""


def run_delete_task(cfg: Config, ref: TaskRef) -> str:
    """Delete one resolved task and return the report line.

    The filesystem removal owns the checkout-local spawn-admission barrier.
    Callers own Git publication: `coga delete` lands the removal immediately;
    recurring replacement recreates the task at the same path and syncs that
    replacement as one state transition.

    `DeleteTaskError` is the *only* failure this raises. Deletion used to run
    behind a subprocess, where a filesystem error surfaced as a non-zero exit
    and became one; in-process, `rmtree`/`unlink` raise `OSError` directly, so
    it is translated here. Every caller — `coga delete`, the recipe, and
    recurring replacement, which runs unattended — catches that one type, and a
    read-only file or a held handle must not abort them with a traceback.
    """
    ticket = ref.ticket_path
    try:
        with git.state_lock(cfg):
            if not ticket.is_file():
                raise DeleteTaskError(
                    f"{ticket} is not a file — refusing to delete"
                )
            if ticket.name == "ticket.md":
                # Directory form: remove the whole task directory (ticket + siblings).
                shutil.rmtree(ticket.parent)
                target: Path = ticket.parent
            else:
                # File form: remove just the single-file ticket; leave the parent
                # (a shared tasks/ subtree) untouched.
                ticket.unlink()
                target = ticket
    except git.GitError as exc:
        raise DeleteTaskError(
            f"could not serialize deletion of {ticket}: {exc}"
        ) from exc
    except OSError as exc:
        raise DeleteTaskError(f"could not delete {ticket}: {exc}") from exc

    return f"{ref.id_slug}: deleted {target}\n"


def run_delete_task_recipe(cfg: Config, argv: list[str]) -> int:
    """`coga run delete-task <task>` — remove one task from the working tree.

    The removal only; landing it on the control branch is `coga delete`'s job.
    """
    if len(argv) != 1 or not argv[0].strip():
        sys.stderr.write(
            "Usage: coga run delete-task <task> — exactly one task ref is "
            f"required (got {len(argv)}).\n"
        )
        return 2

    try:
        ref = resolve_task(cfg, argv[0].strip())
    except TaskNotFoundError as exc:
        sys.stderr.write(f"delete-task: {exc}\n")
        return 2

    try:
        report = run_delete_task(cfg, ref)
    except DeleteTaskError as exc:
        sys.stderr.write(f"delete-task: {exc}\n")
        return 2

    sys.stdout.write(report)
    return 0

import typer

from coga import git

from coga.config import ConfigError, load_config
from coga.delete_task import DeleteTaskError, run_delete_task
from coga.tasks import TaskNotFoundError, resolve_task


def delete(
    task: str = typer.Argument(..., help="Task ID or id-slug."),
    keep_control_checkout: bool = typer.Option(
        False,
        "--keep-control-checkout",
        help=(
            "From a linked worktree, push the deletion without fast-forwarding "
            "another checkout that holds the control branch. Used by Retro."
        ),
    ),
) -> None:
    """Remove a task directory. Recovery is via `git restore`."""
    try:
        cfg = load_config()
    except ConfigError as exc:
        _bail(str(exc))

    try:
        ref = resolve_task(cfg, task)
    except TaskNotFoundError as exc:
        _bail(str(exc))

    if keep_control_checkout and not git.is_linked_worktree(ref.path):
        _bail(
            "--keep-control-checkout requires a linked git worktree; refusing "
            "to delete from the primary checkout"

    try:
        output = run_delete_task(cfg, ref)
    except DeleteTaskError as exc:
        _bail(str(exc))

    try:

            ).rstrip("\n"),
            fg=typer.colors.YELLOW,
            err=True,
        )

    typer.secho(msg, fg=typer.colors.RED, err=True)

   read-only, use an independent `git clone --no-hardlinks` under `/tmp`,
   repointed to the configured real remote. Do not run Retro in this retire
   task's checkout or fall back to an unisolated subagent. Before any Coga
   command, ordinary-copy the caller's gitignored `coga.local.toml` to the same
   repo-relative path in the isolated checkout; never symlink, snapshot, stage,
   or commit it. In the
   isolated subagent, read the skill at
   package `bootstrap/skills/retro/done-ticket/SKILL.md` unless a local
   `coga/skills/retro/done-ticket/SKILL.md` override exists, and follow it.
   The skill verifies the isolated-checkout boundary before reading the snapshot;
   all Retro branch switches and deletes stay inside it. When new durable
   knowledge exists, Retro opens a PR that records the `## Retro` marker, edits
   the knowledge base, and deletes `coga/tasks/{slug}/` in the same PR. When no
   new durable knowledge exists, it runs
   `coga delete {slug} --keep-control-checkout` from a linked worktree or
   ordinary `coga delete {slug}` from an independent clone. Both land the
   direct `Ticket: {slug} — deleted` commit on the remote control branch
   without refreshing the operator's checkout, with no PR and no marker.
   The exception is a ticket that some tracked file still links. It leaves in
   a reference-pin PR that repoints the link to a commit permalink (the skill's
   **Inbound references**). Recovery is via `git restore`.

   After the subagent returns or terminates, read `progress.md`. Without its
   `complete` line, record a partial outcome and retain the run directory and
   isolated checkout. A missing action receipt does not prove the remote was
   unchanged; follow the skill's reconciliation checks before retrying, and
   escalate if the outcome cannot be established. Do not mark this retire task
   done or remove recovery paths on the strength of a final message alone.

   For a completed run, verify the PR branch is pushed or the direct
   deletion is present on the remote control branch, and verify the isolated
   checkout is clean. Remove the copied `coga.local.toml`; then remove the
   linked worktree and its temporary branch, or delete the exact independent
   clone directory. Record the verified outcome on this task's blackboard,
   then delete the temporary run directory (snapshot and progress file) too.
   Mutating subagents are
   not guaranteed to auto-clean. If durability or cleanup cannot be verified,
   preserve both paths and block.

2. **Mark this retire task done.** Run `coga mark done <this-task-slug>`
   with a `--message` summarizing what happened: the retro PR link, or
   "direct-deleted, no durable knowledge or inbound references" for a direct delete.

### Stop conditions

- Source task is not `status: canceled` → escalate via `coga block` with the
  reason. This task only runs Retro on a canceled ticket.
- Source task is missing → first decide **which** kind of missing. If the slug
  is wrong or unknown, escalate.

  Otherwise ask two questions in order.

  **Is it gone from the control branch?** That branch is the authority, not
  your working tree. Retro direct-deletes from a linked worktree with
  `coga delete --keep-control-checkout`, which deliberately leaves the
  operator's checkout untouched, so the source directory can still sit on your
  disk while already being absent from `<remote>/<control-branch>`. Requiring
  absence in both places would send this shell into a Retro run whose fresh
  isolated base lacks the source — which stops, recreating exactly the blocker
  this path exists to avoid. Fetch and check the control branch; a stale local
  copy is not evidence that the task is still live.

  **Did Retro actually process it?** Absence alone does not answer this. Every
  deletion — Retro's and an ordinary user's `coga delete <slug>` — writes the
  same `Ticket: <slug> — deleted` subject, so that commit being an ancestor of
  the control branch proves the directory is gone, not that any knowledge was
  extracted. Closing on the generic commit alone would silently skip Retro and
  discard durable knowledge. Require evidence that ties the deletion to a
  Retro/Dream pass, such as:
  - the deleting commit (or its PR) also adds or updates the source task's
    `## Retro` marker — the knowledge-bearing route;
  - a Dream run's `## Findings` / `## Dream Run Summary`, or a retro PR body,
    naming this slug as processed;
  - a `coga/log.md` line or retro PR recording the no-durable-knowledge
    direct-delete for this slug.

  With absence from the control branch **and** Retro evidence, this shell is
  **orphaned, not broken**: retire's whole contract — knowledge extracted,
  ticket deleted — is already satisfied by the skill this shell exists to
  drive. Record the evidence on this shell's blackboard and `coga mark done`
  it as already satisfied. Do **not** `git restore` the source to rerun Retro,
  and do **not** `coga block` — the missing-source stop condition guards
  against a wrong slug, not against a retirement that already happened.

  With absence but **no** Retro evidence, something deleted the ticket without
  extracting from it. Do not mark this shell done; escalate via `coga block`
  naming the slug and the bare deletion commit, so a human decides whether to
  restore and rerun Retro.
- A complete evidence snapshot, machine-local config copy, or isolated
  worktree/clone execution is unavailable → escalate; never run Retro in this
  task's checkout as a fallback.
- Retro skill stops and asks → surface the reason; do not improvise.
- Anything outside the allowed scope above → escalate, do not improvise.

name: coga-dev/microkernel
description: "Coga core placement: the microkernel rule, open command placement decisions, and moving built-ins to the edge."
